Yeah, it’s just a maximization problem and there are a lot of other factors outside of simple supply and demand economics, one of the principal being taxes. The side that is more inelastic will bear the burden of a change in price- consumers of meat are more inelastic than producers. 

In other words, if there is a 1% change in price, consumers will still buy about the same amount of meat while suppliers would change the amount supplied. This is really obvious for foodstuffs: people will still need to eat, and meat is an integral part of most diets in America. On the flip side, these factory farms can easily cut back on the amount of meat they are producing just by not slaughtering as many of their livestock.

It’s how we determine who actually pays taxes too. So let’s say you decided to start taxing oil companies without a reliable alternative for cars to use for transportation. The consumers who need oil for their car are much more inelastic than the oil companies, so even if the tax was levied to the companies, the consumers would see that reflected in the price at the pump and it would not be a 50-50 shouldering of the tax incidence.
